chunks: And as for what was narrated - Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Jamil ibn Darraj from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding a mukatab (slave who has agreed to pay a sum for his freedom) who dies having paid part of his manumission price, and he has a son from a concubine, and he left wealth, he said: 'His son pays the remainder of his manumission price, and he is freed, and inherits what remains.'

The ruling in it is also what we previously mentioned in the report of another, equally. As for what the report of Malik ibn 'Atiyyah included from his saying: 'If the mukatab leaves nothing, there is no claim on the son,' this is to be understood as meaning there is no claim on him for more than what remained on his father, and it does not all return to slavery, because it is incumbent upon him to strive for what remained on his father so that he becomes free. Indicating that is what was narrated:

key_terms.مُكَاتَبٍ: A slave who has agreed to pay a fixed sum to his master in exchange for freedom
key_terms.مُكَاتَبَتِهِ: The manumission contract or the remaining debt of the mukatab

ai.seo_question: What happens to a mukatab's remaining debt and estate if he dies leaving a son and some wealth?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the apparent contradiction between this report from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id and the narration of Malik ibn Atiyyah by interpreting the latter as limiting the son's liability to the remaining debt rather than imposing a fresh obligation or reverting the father to full slavery. This interpretation underscores the Shia juristic principle that the son's payment of the mukatab's debt serves primarily to secure the father's manumission, after which the son inherits the residual estate as a free heir.
